units:
Digital Image Processing — SVM Worked Example
SVM Image Classification: Apple vs Banana
Step-by-step numerical handout using handcrafted colour feature vectors
Image → Feature Extraction → Feature Vector → SVM → Class Label
1. Handcrafted Feature Vector
For a simple classroom example, represent each image using the mean Red, Green and Blue intensities. For an 
image with N pixels:
R_mean = (1/N) Σ R_p G_mean = (1/N) Σ G_p B_mean = (1/N) Σ B_p
x = [R_mean, G_mean, B_mean]
This converts an image containing thousands of pixel values into a compact 3-dimensional numerical feature 
vector.
2. Training Data
Training image Feature vector x = [R, G, B] Class label y
Apple 1 [210, 70, 55] +1
Apple 2 [205, 65, 50] +1
Banana 1 [225, 205, 60] −1
Banana 2 [230, 210, 70] −1
We choose Apple = +1 and Banana = −1. In this toy dataset, the Green-channel feature already separates the two 
classes clearly:
Apple: G = 65, 70 Banana: G = 205, 210
3. Identify the Closest Training Samples
The nearest Apple to the Banana class has G = 70. The nearest Banana to the Apple class has G = 205. These are 
the support-vector locations in this simplified one-dimensional separation.
G_A = 70 G_B = 205
The maximum-margin decision boundary lies midway between the two support vectors:
G_boundary = (70 + 205)/2 = 137.5
Therefore: G < 137.5 → Apple | G > 137.5 → Banana

Digital Image Processing — SVM Worked Example
4. Linear SVM Equation
For a linear binary SVM:
f(x) = wᵀx + b
where w contains the feature weights and b is the bias. Here:
x = [R, G, B]ᵀ w = [w_R, w_G, w_B]ᵀ
Because this simplified dataset can be separated using only G, choose w_R = 0 and w_B = 0. We solve for w_G and 
b from the support-vector conditions.
5. Solve w and b Step by Step
For a hard-margin SVM, support vectors satisfy y(wᵀx + b) = 1. Therefore:
Apple support vector (G = 70): 70w_G + b = +1 ...(1)
Banana support vector (G = 205): 205w_G + b = −1 ...(2)
Subtract Eq. (1) from Eq. (2):
205w_G − 70w_G = −1 − 1
135w_G = −2
w_G = −2/135 ≈ −0.014815
Substitute into Eq. (1):
(−0.014815)(70) + b = 1
−1.037 + b = 1
b ≈ 2.037
Final model: w = [0, −0.014815, 0] b = 2.037
6. Final Decision Function
f(x) = 0R − 0.014815G + 0B + 2.037
f(x) = 2.037 − 0.014815G
Prediction rule: f(x) > 0 → Apple | f(x) < 0 → Banana

Digital Image Processing — SVM Worked Example
7. Test a New Apple Image
Suppose the new image has feature vector:
x = [208, 68, 52]
Use the learned SVM decision function:
f(x) = 2.037 − 0.014815(68)
f(x) = 2.037 − 1.0074 ≈ 1.030
Since f(x) > 0, the predicted class is APPLE.
8. Test a New Banana Image
Suppose:
x = [228, 208, 65]
f(x) = 2.037 − 0.014815(208)
f(x) = 2.037 − 3.0815 ≈ −1.045
Since f(x) < 0, the predicted class is BANANA.
9. Verify the Decision Boundary
At the decision boundary, f(x) = 0:
2.037 − 0.014815G = 0
G ≈ 137.5
This agrees exactly with the midpoint calculated earlier.
10. Margin Calculation
Distance from the boundary to each support vector:
137.5 − 70 = 67.5 and 205 − 137.5 = 67.5
The full margin between the two supporting hyperplanes is:
Margin = 2 / ||w||
||w|| = 0.014815 ⇒ Margin ≈ 2/0.014815 ≈ 135
This equals 205 − 70 = 135, confirming the geometry.

Digital Image Processing — SVM Worked Example
11. Generalization to Real Image Classification
Real image classification normally uses richer handcrafted features. A complete feature vector may contain 
colour, texture and shape descriptors:
x = [R_mean, G_mean, B_mean, Contrast, Energy, Homogeneity, Correlation, HOG₁, …, HOG_n]
The SVM then learns one weight for each feature:
f(x) = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + … + w_dx_d + b
In software, the SVM optimization automatically identifies the support vectors and learns w and b.
12. Summary
Step Meaning
1 Extract handcrafted features from each image
2 Form a numerical feature vector x
3 Assign class labels (+1 / −1)
4 SVM finds the maximum-margin separating boundary
5 Learn w and b
6 For a new image compute f(x) = wᵀx + b
7 Use the sign of f(x) to assign the class
Key idea: SVM classifies feature vectors by finding a separating hyperplane with the maximum possible 
margin between classes.
Teaching note: This numerical example is intentionally simplified so every calculation can be verified manually.
